Today the umbrella is so ubiquitous that few people stop to wonder where it came from. Yet this modest device has a long and surprisingly [[1]] history that stretches back thousands of years. Over three thousand years ago, umbrellas appeared in ancient Egypt and China, but they were never intended to keep anyone dry. Instead, they provided [[2]] from the scorching sun, and only monarchs, priests, and aristocrats enjoyed the privilege of using them. For centuries, the umbrella remained a [[3]] of prestige rather than an accessory for ordinary citizens.
In China, skilled craftsmen began to coat paper umbrellas with oil and wax so that they could [[4]] heavy downpours. This ingenious improvement gradually traveled along trade routes to other parts of Asia and, much later, to Europe. European gentlemen, however, initially refused to adopt them. They regarded umbrellas as [[5]] objects that only ladies should carry, and a man holding one in public was frequently ridiculed by passersby.
Attitudes began to change in the eighteenth century, largely thanks to a stubborn British traveler named Jonas Hanway. After returning from Persia, he carried an umbrella through the drizzly streets of London for nearly thirty years. Coachmen [[6]] him at first, but he refused to abandon the habit. Eventually, other men followed his example, and the once eccentric practice [[7]] throughout the nation.
The design itself also kept evolving. Early European umbrellas were heavy and clumsy, with frames made of timber or whalebone. In 1852, Samuel Fox introduced a steel frame that was both sturdy and light, making the umbrella far more [[8]] for daily use. Modern collapsible versions can even fold small enough to [[9]] in a coat pocket.
From a royal emblem of power to an everyday tool, the umbrella demonstrates how the meaning of an object can [[10]] as societies and their needs develop.
